name: Information Architecture (IA)
contentMarkdown:
# Information Architecture (IA)

Information architecture (IA) is the organization and labeling of content and functionality so people can find, understand, and use it. In websites and apps, it connects categories, relationships, labels, navigation, and search to the tasks people need to complete.

## What does information architecture include?

IA decisions determine where information belongs and how people reach it. A content model identifies the types of information a product contains. A taxonomy groups that information, and labels give those groups names. Navigation, search, and filters provide ways to find it.

For example, a booking product might treat a Trip as a container for flight bookings, traveler details, and documents. An invoice belongs to a booking, and users may also need to find invoices across several trips. That relationship can support both a link on the booking page and a separate invoice search.

## Example: Finding an invoice

A travel team’s portal puts invoices in a section called “Resources.” Research shows that employees look inside their bookings first. The team adds a clearly named Invoices section to each booking and links it from the booking summary. Search can also retrieve invoices by booking reference.

The proposed structure follows the employee’s task and keeps the same invoice accessible through more than one route. Test whether users can find the invoice, recognize the right booking, and retrieve the document.

## How do you evaluate information architecture?

Start with an inventory of the content and the tasks users need to complete. Card sorting can reveal how participants group and name information. Once a hierarchy is proposed, tree testing evaluates whether people can find a destination using its categories and labels. Test the working interface as well to see whether users notice and understand the navigation.

At enterprise scale, IA also needs shared definitions and ownership across products and teams. See [Enterprise Information Architecture](/glossary/enterprise-information-architecture.html) for that broader scope.

name: Core Model
contentMarkdown:
# Core Model

The Core Model is Are Halland’s method for planning a page or digital experience around the overlap between user tasks and business goals. It connects the content people need with the paths that bring them there and the useful next steps they can take.

## What does a core model contain?

Choose a core page and record its user tasks, business goals, inward paths, core content, and forward paths. These fields help a team decide what the experience must support before working on its layout.

## Example: A hotel room detail page

| Core Model field | Example |
|---|---|
| Core page | Details for a family room. |
| User tasks | Check capacity, bed arrangements, cancellation terms, and availability for the intended dates. |
| Business goals | Help travelers choose a suitable room and complete a booking. |
| Inward paths | A room search result, a saved link, or a search-engine result. |
| Core content | Room capacity, bed types, photos, applicable terms, and availability and price for selected dates. |
| Forward paths | Select dates, book the room, compare another room, or ask a question. |

A traveler entering from a saved link needs enough context to identify the room and select dates. Someone arriving from dated search results expects the price and availability to match those dates. The model makes these entry conditions explicit.

## How do you use the Core Model?

Develop the model with people responsible for user research, content, product, and business outcomes. Use research to establish user tasks, then sketch how the page can support them and the intended next steps.

Test the proposed experience through realistic entry paths. Can a traveler confirm the room fits their party and find the applicable cancellation terms? Can they proceed with their chosen dates? Revisit the model when the test reveals missing information or an onward path that interrupts the task.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)
- [Wayfinding System](/glossary/wayfinding-system.html)
- [Conversion Funnel](/glossary/conversion-funnel-architecture.html)
- [Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)](/glossary/jobs-to-be-done-jtbd.html)

name: Enterprise Information Architecture
contentMarkdown:
# Enterprise Information Architecture

Enterprise information architecture (EIA) organizes information across an organization’s products, repositories, and services so people can find, understand, and use it. It connects shared vocabulary, classification, metadata, navigation, search, and governance across teams and systems.

In UX practice, this includes intranets, employee portals, and business applications. Teams coordinate definitions across owners and workflows: the same customer, policy, or expense claim may appear in several places.

## What does enterprise information architecture include?

| Area | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Shared vocabulary | Do teams mean the same thing by “customer,” “account,” or “approved”? |
| Taxonomy and metadata | How is information classified, described, filtered, and retrieved? |
| Objects and relationships | How do records connect to people, documents, and other records? |
| Navigation and search | How can users reach information across products and repositories? |
| Governance | Who owns definitions, resolves conflicts, and maintains the structure? |

Access rules also shape what different users can find and see. Shared definitions can support different role-specific views without requiring every team to use the same navigation.

## An enterprise IA example: expense claims

Consider an illustrative employee portal connected to an expense system. An employee submits Claim #482; a manager reviews it; finance processes reimbursement.

The team defines one claim identifier and distinguishes **Submitted**, **Approved**, and **Paid**. Approval means the manager accepted the claim; payment means reimbursement was completed. That distinction needs to remain clear wherever the claim appears.

| User | Entry point | Information needed |
|---|---|---|
| Employee | My expenses | Claim status, receipts, and payment date |
| Manager | Claims awaiting approval | Amount, policy, and supporting receipts |
| Finance | Approved claims | Payment details and reimbursement status |

These views refer to the same claim. Links connect it to its receipts and the relevant policy. Metadata such as owner, date, and status supports search and filtering.

An assigned owner maintains the status definitions and checks how changes affect each system.

## How do you start?

Start with one task that crosses a team or system boundary. Interview the people involved, inventory the records and content they use, and note conflicting labels or duplicate sources.

Agree on definitions and ownership with domain experts. Identify the authoritative source for each record or policy. Then prototype navigation, search results, and record relationships. Use card sorting to explore groupings, tree testing to check findability, and usability testing to evaluate the complete task.

Measure whether people find the right information and complete the task accurately. Search failures, wrong destinations, and time spent locating records can reveal structural problems.

## How is enterprise IA different from a sitemap?

A sitemap describes a hierarchy of pages. Enterprise IA also coordinates meaning, metadata, relationships, and ownership across systems. One deliverable might be a sitemap; others include a vocabulary, taxonomy, content model, or governance plan. The appropriate structure depends on users’ work and the information involved.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)

name: Mental Model Mapping
contentMarkdown:
# Mental Model Mapping

Mental model mapping is a research and synthesis practice for representing how people understand, approach, and make decisions about an activity or system. Designers use it to identify where a product supports those expectations and where gaps or mismatches occur.

A mental model reflects a person's understanding; it can be incomplete or differ from how the system actually works. Research is needed to distinguish observed expectations from a team's assumptions.

## How to build a useful map

Gather accounts of real experiences through interviews and, where appropriate, observation. Look for recurring goals, reasoning, expectations, and workarounds. Preserve meaningful differences between people.

Indi Young's mental model diagrams organize patterns in people's thinking and compare them with the support an organization provides. That is one established approach; teams should name the method they use.

## Example: planning a family trip

Research might show that travelers first work out school-date constraints, then compare total trip cost, and only later choose specific flights.

A map could group those activities and the reasoning behind them. The team could compare each group with existing support: a date picker, fare results, baggage information, and a saved-trip feature.

If users expect the displayed price to include baggage while the product adds it later, the mismatch becomes a concrete design question to investigate.

## Keep the evidence visible

Link the map to research observations and label hypotheses. Avoid treating a navigation tree or an internally invented persona as evidence of users' thinking.

A task model describes activities and dependencies. Mental model mapping examines the understanding and reasoning behind behavior; the two can inform each other. Update the map when new research challenges its patterns.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)
- [Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)](/glossary/jobs-to-be-done-jtbd.html)
- [Task Model](/glossary/task-model.html)
- [Conceptual Schema](/glossary/conceptual-schema.html)

name: Content Modeling
contentMarkdown:
# Content Modeling

Content modeling defines the types of content a product needs, the fields that describe them, and how they relate to one another. A content model also records rules that help editors create consistent entries and lets products reuse that content across pages and channels.

## What does a content model include?

| Part | Example decision |
|---|---|
| Content type | Represent a hotel’s Room Type as a reusable type of content. |
| Fields | Store the room type’s name, capacity, description, and photos. |
| References | Link the room type to Hotel and Amenity entries. |
| Validation | Require a name and capacity, and restrict an Amenity reference to the appropriate content type. |

The model describes the structure. An entry contains the actual content, such as the description and photos for a Family Room.

## Example: Reusing room content on a hotel site

A hotel uses the same Family Room content in a results card and a room detail page. The card shows the name, capacity, and lead photo. The detail page uses those fields plus the description, gallery, and amenity references.

Both views read the same room entry. Updating a shared Amenity entry gives consuming views a consistent source for its wording. Publishing and delivery determine when that update appears. The implementation controls which fields are displayed and how.

Treat the current price and availability as booking data with their own update requirements. The content model can identify the room type that the booking system uses when it returns those values.

## How do you develop a content model?

Inventory representative content and discuss publishing needs with editors, designers, and developers. Define the types and references, then test them with realistic entries. Include a room with a long name, missing optional content, and localized text if the product supports it.

Have an editor create and update an entry, then review it in each consuming view. Check whether the model supports the intended content without duplicating information or forcing editors to use a field for an unrelated purpose.
